neutral_facts.value: The accused, who were relatives of the victim, trespassed into the victim's house, concealed iron rods, and brutally killed the victim and his wife. They robbed gold ornaments and cash from the house. The victim's son and wife were found dead in the house with signs of violent injuries. The police arrested the accused shortly after the incident, recovered stolen property, and conducted an investigation. Witnesses reported seeing the accused fleeing the scene with bags. The prosecution presented circumstantial evidence, including witness statements, medical reports, and recovered items, to establish the accused's guilt. The trial court convicted the accused, and the High Court upheld the conviction.

prosecution_argument.value: The complainant, PW-1, stated that the accused trespassed into his house, concealed iron rods, and brutally killed his son and wife, robbed gold ornaments and cash, and the police recovered stolen property from the accused. The prosecution argued that the circumstantial evidence, along with medical evidence, weapons used, and the manner of attack, established the accused's intent to cause death.

quotes.text: The complainant, Vetcha Kesava Rao (PW-1), is a resident of Ichapuram and his house is situated on Chinnamedaraveedhi, wherein he also did his gold and silver business.
The prosecution examined 27 witnesses and marked Exs.P-1 to P-21 in evidence, apart from producing Material Objects (MOs) 1 to 99.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that there were discrepancies and contradictions in the prosecution's case, including the sequence of events at the scene of the offence, the testimonies of witnesses, and the recovery of clothes worn by the accused. They also questioned the evidentiary value of the witnesses' statements regarding the accused running away with bags.

quotes.text: The accused did not adduce evidence but were examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Upon considering the evidence and the MOs, the learned VI Additional District and Sessions Judge, Sompeta, held the accused guilty of the offences punishable under Sections 302, 397 and 450 IPC.
There are no eye-witnesses to the actual commission of the offence and the case is built on circumstantial evidence.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that in cases of circumstantial evidence, the chain of evidence must be so complete as to not leave any reasonable grounds for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused. The court also emphasized that the Trial Court and High Court's findings of fact cannot be reappreciated unless there is a manifest illegality or miscarriage of justice.

quotes.text: In such a situation, the chain of evidence must be so complete as to not leave any reasonable grounds for a conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused;

It was observed that it is only if the assessment by the Trial Court and the High Court can be said to be vitiated by any error of law or procedure or misreading of evidence or in disregard to the norms of judicial process, leading to serious prejudice or injustice, that this Court may, and in appropriate cases would, interfere.

precedent_relied_upon.value: Pappu vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh (2022) 10 SCC 321; Sambhu Das alias Bijoy Das and another Vs. State of Assam (2010) 10 SCC 374; Hanumant Govind Nargundkar Vs. State of M.P. AIR 1952 SC 343; Karnel Singh Vs. State of M.P. (1995) 5 SCC 518

quotes.text: In Pappu Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh [(2022) 10 SCC 321], this Court pointed out that, in an appeal by special leave under Article 136 of the Constitution against concurrent findings of fact by the Trial Court and the High Court after appreciation of evidence, each and every finding of fact cannot be contested and such an appeal cannot be dealt with as if this Court is another forum for reappreciation of evidence.

In Sambhu Das alias Bijoy Das and another Vs. State of Assam [(2010) 10 SCC 374], this Court affirmed that Article 136 of the Constitution does not confer a right of appeal on a party and only confers discretionary power on this Court to be exercised sparingly to interfere in suitable cases where grave miscarriage of justice has resulted from illegality or misapprehension or mistake in reading evidence or from ignoring, excluding or illegally admitting material evidence.

sentencing_rationale.value: The final sentence was imposed because the Trial Court and High Court found the accused guilty of the offences punishable under Sections 302, 397, and 450 IPC, and the Supreme Court found no patent illegality or manifest injustice in the sentencing.

quotes.text: The Trial Court and the High Court found the accused guilty of the offences punishable under Sections 302, 397, and 450 IPC, and the Supreme Court found no patent illegality or manifest injustice in the sentencing.

The accused were sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life under Section 302 IPC and to pay fine of ¹ 2,000/- each; imprisonment for a period of 10 years under Section 450 IPC and to pay a fine of ¹ 2,000/- each; and imprisonment for 7 years under Section 397 IPC.
